source.title: LLM Jailbreak Detection for (Almost) Free!
source.authors: Guo-Rui Chen; Yi-Fan Xia; Xiao-Jun Jia; Zhijiang Li; P. Torr; Jindong Gu

record.file_problem: none; full paper text and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses first-token confidence differences to build and evaluate a jailbreak detector. It does not test safety refusal/compliance rates, aligned-versus-base per-token KL across response positions, or whether generation prefills bypass refusal.
record.gate_note: The measured outcomes are first-token confidence distributions and jailbreak-detection AUC, not harmful-completion or refusal rates. The paper cites prior claims about jailbreaks and safety but does not test the claim versions here. Rows record its own first-token confidence and detection results as related findings; detection AUC is not evidence of model compliance.
record.test_reason: The study builds a jailbreak-prompt detector from first-token confidence and reports only detector AUC/FPR/TPR. It measures no harmful-compliance or refusal rates, no aligned-vs-base per-token KL, no fine-tuning, no prefill or decoding attack success, and no deepening training. First-token confidence differences between jailbreak and benign prompts are a related construct, not V3's aligned-vs-base KL.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that first-token confidence, boosted by affirmative-instruction prepending and temperature scaling, detects jailbreak prompts efficiently at almost no extra inference cost, and that learned virtual instructions (FJD-LI) improve it further. Stated limitations: weaker results on GCG than perplexity detection, vulnerability to white-box detection-aware attacks, and model-dependent performance.
record.recipe_differences: The paper evaluates a confidence-based detection method using prompt prepending and temperature scaling, not fine-tuning safety behavior or measuring aligned-versus-base KL across response positions.
record.method_sensitivity: Detection outcomes vary by model and jailbreak attack; affirmative instructions and temperature affect detector performance. The paper states temperature has a substantial impact around 0.5 and tests temperatures over [0, 2].

fits_no_version.finding: In aligned 7B chat models, jailbreak prompts (GCG, AutoDAN, Cipher) yield lower first-token max-probability than benign prompts. Shown in figures only, no numbers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: First-token output confidence differs between jailbreak and benign prompts in aligned LLMs.

fits_no_version.finding: A first-token confidence detector with an affirmative-instruction prefix and temperature scaling separates jailbreak from benign prompts. AUC ranges from about 0.75 to 0.99, varies by model and attack, and the detector is broken by white-box detection-aware attacks (AUC 0.476 on Vicuna-7B).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: First-token confidence enables low-cost jailbreak-prompt detection.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: Detector AUC is not a direct measure of harmful response rates or safety refusal. The paper reports that detection-aware white-box attacks can impair FJD, and notes model-dependent sensitivity. Some first-token distribution evidence is presented only in figures without numerical values.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix tables and additional experiments report further detector AUC results (including GCG, MAC, PAIR, hand-crafted, transfer, FJD-LI, and multimodal settings). These were not extracted because they remain detection-performance measures rather than safety-behavior outcomes; the main-text model-by-attack FJD results and the directly described first-token comparisons are retained.

untested.parts: No harmful fine-tuning or compliance rates.
No aligned-vs-base per-token KL by position. Only first-token max-probability for jailbreak vs benign prompts in aligned models.
Jailbreak prompts are used as inputs, but no attack success, refusal or harmful-completion rates are reported, including for prefix-injection hand-crafted attacks.
Appendix D offers only hypotheses (attention hijack, OOD, residual refusal probability), untested against data or objective.

record.verdict_notes: Appendix O / Fig. 9 report that averaging confidence over the first k tokens sometimes helps and hurts for AutoDAN. This is about detection signal over positions, not safety-alignment depth, and is not V3 evidence. The study cites Qi et al. 2310.03693 only as a reference. Not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: No fine-tuning on harmful examples or harmful-request refusal/compliance rate is measured.
No fine-tuning on benign instruction data or resulting harmful-request compliance rate is measured.
No aligned-versus-base per-token KL divergence or distribution of KL across response positions is measured.

The paper prepends affirmative instructions to user queries, but does not test generation prefills of compliant opening tokens, nor report harmful-completion rates after prefills, suffixes, or decoding changes.
No safety weights or ranks are localized or edited.
The study does not investigate why safety behavior is shallow or test the effects of safety-training data or objectives on shallowness.
No training to deepen safety behavior or robustness of such training is tested.

rows.subject: Llama2 7B
rows.operation_detail: Compared predicted first-token confidence distributions for jailbreak and benign prompts.
rows.note: The text says jailbreak prompts have lower first-token confidence than benign prompts; no numerical distribution values are stated.
rows.check: Figure-only first-token confidence comparison, jailbreak vs benign. Not aligned-vs-base KL, so it does not bear on V3. A state of 'observed' is meaningless with versions none. Same applies to R2–R11.
